entities.summary: Ibrāhīm al-Fazārī was an Arab philosopher, mathematician, and astronomer born in the 8th century CE, who flourished during the Classical era and had a significant impact on the development of Islamic thought and science. Born in Baghdad, Iraq, he was a key figure in the House of Wisdom, a renowned center of learning that attracted scholars from across the Islamic world. His philosophical works, which included commentaries on Aristotle and a treatise on the nature of the universe, influenced thinkers such as Al-Khwarizmi and Ibn Sina, shaping the course of Islamic philosophy and science for centuries to come. Al-Fazārī's contributions to mathematics, particularly in the field of algebra, also had far-reaching consequences, as his work on the solution of linear and quadratic equations laid the foundation for later mathematicians such as Al-Khwarizmi. His writings on astronomy, including a treatise on the movements of the planets, further advanced the understanding of celestial mechanics and paved the way for later astronomical discoveries. Despite his significant impact on the development of Islamic thought and science, Ibrāhīm al-Fazārī's work was largely forgotten in the West until the 19th century, when scholars such as Auguste Courteville rediscovered and translated his writings. Today, al-Fazārī is recognized as one of the most important figures in the history of Islamic philosophy and science, and his contributions continue to inspire scholars and researchers around the world.

entities.summary:
Ibrāhīm al-Fazārī (ibrhm-al-fazr) was an Arab philosopher, mathematician and astronomer born in unknown and died in 777 CE in Baghdad, Iraq. 

He was a key figure in the development of Islamic mathematics and astronomy, making significant contributions to algebra, geometry, and trigonometry. His most notable work is the book "Kitab al-Manazir" (The Book of Optics), which deals with the nature of light and vision.

Ibrāhīm al-Fazārī's work had a profound impact on the development of Islamic science and learning, influencing scholars such as Ibn Sina and Ibn Rushd. His discoveries and theories on optics, geometry, and mathematics laid the groundwork for later scientific advancements in the Islamic Golden Age.

One of Ibrāhīm al-Fazārī's most enduring legacies is the transmission of ancient Greek knowledge to the Islamic world, which had a lasting impact on the development of European science.



Ibrāhīm al-Fazārī was a prolific writer and translator, producing works in Arabic and Persian that were later translated into Latin, Greek, and other languages.



His philosophical and mathematical contributions continue to inspire scholars and scientists to this day, cementing his place as one of the most important figures in the history of Islamic science.
